The previous workshop on environmental tobacco saoke
(Rylanger 1974) concluded that the main acute effect of exposure
to ETS is irritation of the eyes and the respiratory passage.

The extent of this non-specific reaction in the general popula-

tion and the levels at which it occurs are not known. The effects
may occur at very low concentrations among atopic persons or

persons who otherwise have a reactive respiratory tract. Frequently,
such persons also react to low concentrations of other irritating
agents in the environsent, such as dusts and vapors.

It was recommended that the proportion of such reactive
persons in the population be determined as well as the levels at
which these reactions occur, Research was also suggested to
determine whether the reaction is allergic in nature or represents
@ non-specific response occurring at low concentrations of exposure.

According to some researchers, effects other than acute
irritation may occur in certain population groups. The data
Presented, though suggestive of other effects, were not considered
conclusive and more information was deemed necessary.

overall growth in sales has been due mainly to changes inthe size and
composition of the smoking-age population.

events or conditions: the first publicity on smcking and health (1953),

mith restrictions on smoking (197S-).

on total cigarette sales or consumption inthe U.S. Over any period of
about five years, especially for recent years, growth in industry sales is
almost negligibie. s

Bris note details concerns regarding Mike Moore's memo (see attached) requesting his
Brand Group to conduct a senes of analyses using BD! and CDI calculations.
Historically, we have ased SDs to compare brand and category performance across
geographies, and in this the cigarette industry is somewhat unique. First, unlike other
consumer gos categories, shipment data for sll comperitve manufacturers is available at
neatly every geographic level. Second. othe categories tend to have CDI which vary
significandy moore an smoking incidence, Stat Wo sate variation in smoking incidence is
+/-4% of less, across almost all the U.S
The concerns about the proposed analyses center on the methoxlology used 10 calculate
these indices. Cigareste BT's and CDI's are based on two elements
unit consumption in a specified geography
population 18+ in the same geography
However, for the cigarette category, there is no accurate source available for consumption
below the national level
Although shipment data could be viewed as a surrogate for consumption, shipments are
distorted by transshipments (e.g. distibutors in one Section supplying stores in ano:her
Section), and by trade programs
‘Toillustrase how transshipments diston a BDUVCDI calculation:
SPACE estimates treasshipments in a given Section to be 30% incoming. and 6%
outgoing, In other words, 30% of the retal volume sold by reales in the Section is
Supplied by distributors whose warehouses are outside the Section while the remaining
70% is supplied by distributors located within the Section. The SPACE data also indicate
that 6% of all direct shipments to distributors within the Section are eventually delivered to
stores outside the Section, leaving the remaining 94% to be supplied to local retailers.
If shipments to direct accounts in a Section totaled 100 cases, 94 woul! be sold by retailers
in the Section. Since these 94 cases represent 70% of total estimated retail volume,
consumption in the Section would be approximately 134 cases
This means that actual consumption would be 34% greater than shipment data would
indicate, At levels smaller than Sections, ic.,trading areas and DMA‘, where
transshipments end to be greater, the distarions of Consumption rates increase, and often
exceed 100% (see attached exampics). x
Since SDT are calculated off only one data source (factory shipments), any over: or =
understatement will not result in major distortions. BDI's rely on two independent data =
soarces (popalation and shipments), and any overstatement in one will impact the resultant =
ratio of the two. &

Yttrtum (¥), Ytterbium (Yb) and Europtun (Eu), although this toxicity inforn-
tion generally applies to the entire sertes of rare earths (RE).

RE generally have a low order of toxicity by the oral route with LOso
values (lethal dose to SC% of the population) of greater than $ g/kg tn rats.
The RE chlorides, nitrates and oxides are not well absorbed from the gastroin-
testinal tract ‘(approximately 1%). The toxicity when admintstered tn.
traperitoneally was uch greater, with LOso values ranging from 0.3 to 0.6 9/
kg (Haley, 1965). RE tend to form complexes with proteins causing a precipi-
tate to form, In one series of studtes, rats consuming dlets containing 0.01,
0.1 or 1% of a lanthanide for 12 weeks, showed only non-specific ver damage
at the 1% dose (Clayton et. al., 1981). In another chronic study, YC13 was
injected intraperitoneally for $ months (dose not stated) and did not produce
adverse health effects (Bruce et. al., 1963)

Only one inhalation study concerning RE toxicity was found. In this
study, rats were given $0 mg Y203 tntratracheally. After 8 months, granuloma-
tous nodules conststing of crystalline deposits of the oxide with cellular
elenents were present in the lung. This study alone fs not very useful tn

Geep into the trachea). The oxides are also considered much more toxic thas

Based on this scant. evidence, the Anerican Conference of Governnental
Industrial Hygienists (ACGIH) has set a threshold limtt value (TLV) of 1 9g/
(present as Y) for yttrium compounds. There are no specific TLV’s for other
RE. This TLV ts based on an average exposure to workers over the course of an
8-hour working day (ACGIM, 1985)

Based on the lack of tnformation on the inhalation of RE compounds,
Scientific Affairs recommends that additional information be obtained before a
final determination can be made regarding this project. A pilot study should
be conducted to determine both the content of the RE tn the final tobacco

March 17, 1999
Thank you,
Tam honored to be here this evening to offer my warmest
congratulations to the Fifth Graduating Class of the Philip Morris
Agricultural Leadership Development Program.
As we approach the twenty-first century, the issues of agriculture
continue to become more and more complex. I want to ask you to think
back with me. ‘Think back to when we were kids, playing on the big
tractor. In my case the tractor wasn’t all that big and it sure didn’t have
an air-conditioned cab, but it was still mighty impressive to me. Did you
ever once imagine that one day you would need to know almost as much
as a rocket scientist to farm? | don’t know about you, but the concept of
global positioning satellite photos telling me where to put micronutrients
Just didn’t come to mind. Nor did | see much need to take a typing class
in high school. ] had no vision at all of a spreadsheet on a computer
screen. Yet here we are, on the edge of technica) and business
knowledge our great-grandfathers never dreamed of, with opportunities
we don't even see yet. What a fantastic challenge lies before us.

From your memos of July 2 and 22 regarding Reynolds Metals and
alumina, we suspect there are some misconceptions in your mind
which ought to be cleared up.
Alumina {s an aluminum oxide in dehydrated gel form which has had
widespread application in two distinctively different ways: First,
Decause it 1s an excellent adsorber, particularly for water vapor, it
1s often used as a dehydrating agent much like silica gel. Secondly,
decause the alumina gel has a large amount of internal surface, it
may be used as a catalyst for chemical reactions at elevated tempera-
tures. In the petroleum industry many hydrocarbon reactions are
catalyzed by alumina. As a catalyst it might be used to increase the
reaction rate between oxygen and an organic material at some specified
temperature lower than that at which combustion normally occurs.

This last application is the one which Reynolds Metals people
have in mind in their study of alumina as applied to tobacco. Their
application stems from the early work which Dr. Frankenberg at
General Cigar carried on trying to change the combustion character-
Istics of tobacco leaf. When I was at C. H. Dexter Company last
summer the Reynolds Metals people were there in connection with
incorporating alumina into the Dexter homogenized tobacco cigar
“wrapper. Dr. Irving Totten, Director of Research at Reynolds Metals,
has informed me that at present they are awalting reaults of pathological -
tests of the affect of alumina on reduction of toxic materials in tobacco
smoke.

‘The Research Department has, since 1966, been active in the
area of evaluating alumina and similar materials in collaboration with ~~
Minerals and Chemicals Corporation. This Company, through patents
obtained by their Dr. Haden, appears to have a fairly stroog and broad 3
patent position ia the field. Our evaluation of thelr materials indicates
that something like 4% of an alumina-like catalyst would lower the i?
T.P.M. delivery of the cigarette by about 25%. One of the problems
